Can This LLM Annotate My Data?
Estimating Zero-Shot LLM Performance

Tong Lin Affiliation: School of Information, University of Michigan Email: tonglin@umich.edu    Grant Schoenebeck Affiliation: School of Information, University of Michigan Email: schoeneb@umich.edu    Sabina Tomkins Affiliation: School of Information, University of Michigan Email: stomkins@umich.edu
Abstract

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in annotation tasks with varying success. While several studies have demonstrated the opportunities and shortcomings of LLMs for annotation, a critical question remains unanswered: is it possible to predict how well they will perform on a new dataset? To answer this and related questions, we construct two task families which induce 461 text classification datasets. We find that it is possible to predict LLM performance - to a certain degree - and that contrary to other work which highlights the usefulness of LLM verbalizations of self-confidence, internal log-probabilities are the most predictive signal.

1 Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as annotators to produce labeled data at scale for natural language processing (NLP) and the social sciences (Gilardi et al., 2023; Ziems et al., 2024). Yet in many settings, a practical question arises before annotation begins: given a dataset, how well will an LLM label the data under a reasonable prompting setup? Answering this question early matters as annotation pipelines often require substantial investment such as collecting gold labels or human spot-checking, and the costs of misjudging annotation quality can propagate into downstream modeling and scientific conclusions.

One way to answer this question is to look at signals the LLM already produces while it labels. A growing body of work studies such signals for flagging individual incorrect predictions. Answering this instance-level question is useful for selective prediction (Chen et al., 2023), or for routing individual hard cases to human review (Wang et al., 2024b). But that alone does not answer the question a practitioner facing a new, unlabeled dataset needs answered: not “which predictions are wrong,” but “is this dataset labeled reliably enough to use?” A few studies estimate a model’s accuracy on a new dataset (Garg et al., 2022; Fu et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024a; Chen et al., 2025), but each focuses on a single kind of signal. It remains unclear which signals best support such a decision and how many instances are needed. Thus we ask:

  • •

    Can LLM-derived signals support actionable decisions about LLM labeling?

  • •

    Which signals best support decisions about whether LLM labeling is reliable for a dataset?

  • •

    How does the number of sampled instances influence these decisions?

To answer these questions we create two task families which allow us to generate 461 text classification datasets with metadata-derived ground truth: (1) headline topic differentiation and (2) movie script genre classification. We then vary the number of instances sampled from each dataset to understand how much data is needed to predict whether an LLM can label it with at least a certain accuracy. We contribute the following:

  • •

    We find that we can predict whether an LLM will have classification accuracy of at least 0.9 better than trivial baselines for all three LLMs we test (with gains of 10-25% over baselines).

  • •

    We consistently see that internal probability signals perform better than verbalized signals generated by the LLM.

  • •

    We find that there are diminishing returns after ∼\sim100 sampled instances, that is, performance can often be predicted well with only ∼\sim100 samples.

Related Work

LLM annotation quality varies across datasets and tasks (Pangakis et al., 2023), and annotation errors can distort downstream conclusions (Baumann et al., 2025). The common practice is to compare LLM labels against human annotations, either to validate the LLM (Pangakis et al., 2023; Calderon et al., 2025) or to debias the analyses built on LLM labels (Egami et al., 2023). Another line of work estimates the reliability of individual predictions from signals the LLM produces while labeling: token probabilities (Kadavath et al., 2022), consistency across repeated runs (Manakul et al., 2023; Kuhn et al., 2023) and verbalized confidence (Lin et al., 2022; Tian et al., 2023; Xiong et al., 2024). However, insights on which family of signals is most informative about LLM annotation performance are mixed: for example, Tian et al. (2023) find verbalized confidence better calibrated than token probabilities, whereas Xiong et al. (2024) find it overconfident and concentrated on a few values (Merdjanovska et al., 2026). None of this work compares different signals at the dataset level.

Closer to our work, Chen et al. (2025) show that a score based on output consistency tracks annotation accuracy across datasets and Wang et al. (2024a) use likelihood and perplexity features for the same purpose. Fu et al. (2023) train a dataset-level meta-model that maps the distribution of probability scores in a dataset to its accuracy. ATC (Garg et al., 2022) instead works at the instance level by estimating a new dataset’s accuracy as the share of its instances whose confidence exceeds a cutoff learned on labeled data. We advance this work with a comprehensive comparison of the signals which predict LLM annotation performance.

2 Our Approach

Let D={x1,…,xn}D=\{x_{1},\dots,x_{n}\} be a dataset of instances, each requiring a label from a task-specific label set 𝒴\mathcal{Y}. An LLM annotator ℓ\ell is prompted to label each xix_{i}; querying ℓ\ell multiple times per instance and aggregating the responses (by majority vote) yields a predicted label y^i\hat{y}_{i}.

Alongside y^i\hat{y}_{i}, this process yields a signal vector sis_{i} for each instance. Crucially, sis_{i} requires neither a gold label nor any inspection of xix_{i}’s content beyond what ℓ\ell already used to produce y^i\hat{y}_{i}.

We define a dataset’s accuracy as how well ℓ\ell’s aggregated predictions match the ground truth:

R(D)=1n∑i=1n𝟙[y^i=yi].R(D)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathds{1}[\hat{y}_{i}=y_{i}].

In our experiments every dataset has gold labels yiy_{i}, so R⁡(D)R(D) is computable. We define a dataset’s reliability as the binary indicator

r(D)=𝟙[R(D)≥τ],r(D)=\mathds{1}[R(D)\geq\tau],

for a threshold τ\tau reflecting a practitioner’s tolerance for label noise: DD is reliable if ℓ\ell’s labels on it are accurate enough to use, and unreliable otherwise.

We study a collection of MM such datasets 𝒟={D(1),…,D(M)}\mathcal{D}=\{D^{(1)},\dots,D^{(M)}\}, each independently labeled by ℓ\ell following the procedure above, with its own reliability label r⁡(D(m))r(D^{(m)}). Our goal is to predict r⁡(D)r(D) for a held-out dataset D∈𝒟D\in\mathcal{D} from the signals of κ\kappa instances Sκ​(D)S_{\kappa}(D) sampled from it, with no access to their gold labels or to the content of DD. We do this in two stages (Figure 1). First, an instance-level classifier gg learns whether the LLM labels an instance correctly: given the signals sis_{i} of an instance, it outputs the probability g⁡(si)g(s_{i}) that y^i=yi\hat{y}_{i}=y_{i}. It is trained on κ\kappa sampled instances from each training dataset of the fold. Second, we turn these instance-level predictions into a dataset-level decision. Following ATC (Garg et al., 2022), we estimate the accuracy of DD as the share of its sampled instances that gg predicts to be correct,

R^κ(D)=1κ∑xi∈Sκ​(D)𝟙[g(si)≥t],\hat{R}_{\kappa}(D)=\frac{1}{\kappa}\sum_{x_{i}\in S_{\kappa}(D)}\mathds{1}[g(s_{i})\geq t],

and predict DD to be reliable if R^κ​(D)≥τ\hat{R}_{\kappa}(D)\geq\tau. The cutoff tt is set on the training instances so that the share of them with g⁡(si)≥tg(s_{i})\geq t equals their accuracy. We report results separately for gg restricted to different subsets of signals.

2.1 Predictive Signals (Features)

For each instance xix_{i} in each D(m)D^{(m)}, ℓ\ell is queried kk times, yielding a label and its associated signals for each run j=1,…,kj=1,\dots,k.

Internal Probability.

Each run jj exposes the log-probability ℓ\ell assigned to the tokens of its label y^i(j)\hat{y}_{i}^{(j)}. We record two quantities, averaged across the kk runs and negated so higher values indicate greater uncertainty: the log-probability of the label’s first token (writing wi,1(j)w^{(j)}_{i,1} for the first token of y^i(j)\hat{y}_{i}^{(j)}),

uncertaintyfirst(xi)=−1k∑j=1klogpj(wi,1(j)),\operatorname{uncertainty}_{\mathrm{first}}(x_{i})=-\frac{1}{k}\sum_{j=1}^{k}\log p_{j}\big(w^{(j)}_{i,1}\big),

and the average log-probability across all tokens of the label,

uncertaintyavg(xi)=−1k∑j=1klog⁡pj¯(y^i(j)).\operatorname{uncertainty}_{\text{avg}}(x_{i})=-\frac{1}{k}\sum_{j=1}^{k}\overline{\log p_{j}}\big(\hat{y}_{i}^{(j)}\big).

Both require access to the log-probability ℓ\ell assigns to its own output tokens, which open-weight models and some APIs (here GPT-4o mini) expose.

Label Consistency.

Alongside the internal probability signals, we compute one label consistency signal, self-agreement: the fraction of the kk runs whose label matches the majority-vote label y^i\hat{y}_{i},

agreement(xi)=1k∑j=1k𝟙[y^i(j)=y^i].\operatorname{agreement}(x_{i})=\frac{1}{k}\sum_{j=1}^{k}\mathds{1}\big[\hat{y}_{i}^{(j)}=\hat{y}_{i}\big].

Verbalized Signals.

Beyond the label, ℓ\ell is also prompted in the same structured response to self-report a confidence score and a stability score on each run (see Appendix A). We average these across kk runs to obtain two signals:, confidence⁡(xi)\operatorname{confidence}(x_{i}) and stability⁡(xi)\operatorname{stability}(x_{i}); stability is ℓ\ell’s own estimate of how likely it is to assign the same label again. We retrain gg for each κ\kappa, where each dataset contributes κ\kappa instances in training and testing.

3 Experiments

We build two families of text classification tasks whose ground truth comes from structured metadata. Together, these two families give M=110+351=461M=110+351=461 datasets, and let us test whether signal-based reliability estimation holds up under two distinct types of tasks where we can manipulate the difficulty level (e.g. by varying the amount of input data or topic similarity).

Sliding-window genre pairs.

We use movie scripts paired with each film’s genre listing (IsmaelMousa, 2024). For each pair of genres, we take only movies tagged with exactly one of the two genres, excluding movies tagged with both as ambiguous, and ask an LLM which of the two genres the movie belongs to, given all or part of its script. We select 11 genre pairs, each with 247–287 usable movies and at least 38 of each genre (Appendix B), and generate 10 script-length variants per pair: the full script (capped at 50,000 words) and 9 partial versions covering 10%–90% of that capped script, each truncated to the nearest sentence boundary. This yields 11×10=11011\times 10=110 datasets.

NYT topic pairs.

We use the Comparative Agendas Project’s coding of New York Times front-page articles into one of 27 major-topic policy categories (Baumgartner et al., 2019). Given only an article’s headline, an LLM must decide which of the two topics it belongs to. We construct one dataset for every pair of the 27 topics present in the data, which results in 351351 pairs in total, ranging from topically distant pairs (e.g., Defense vs. Churches and Religion) to closely related ones (e.g., Macroeconomics vs. Banking, Finance, and Domestic Commerce). Each dataset has 300 instances.

3.1 Evaluation

In our experiments, ℓ\ell is instantiated as three LLMs: GPT-4o mini, accessed via the OpenAI API (OpenAI, 2024), and the open-weight Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (Grattafiori et al., 2024) and Qwen3-8B (Yang et al., 2025), each labeling every instance k=5k=5 times at temperature 1. For instance-level classifier gg, we test SVM, histogram-based gradient-boosted trees (HGB), and XGBoost. Because our datasets reuse texts (e.g., each NYT topic contributes the same 150 articles to all 26 of its pairs, and each genre pair appears at ten script lengths), we use grouped cross-validation so that no test text appears in training (see Appendix C).

We use τ=0.9\tau=0.9 as the reliability threshold; 74.0%, 36.2%, and 54.4% of the 461 datasets reach it for GPT-4o mini, Llama-3.1-8B, and Qwen3-8B. For each κ∈{10,50,…,210}\kappa\in\{10,50,\dots,210\}, we report the metrics over the pooled held-out predictions and average them over three random seeds.

Table 1 summarizes the results for GPT-4o mini as the annotator, with HGB as gg (see Appendix F for all classifiers and LLMs). Combining all five signals is not the best choice since generally the internal probability or label consistency signals alone do better. The first-token uncertainty is the strongest signal from κ=130\kappa=130 on and reaches an F1 of .875 at κ=210\kappa=210, with most of the gain reached by κ=130\kappa=130. The average-token uncertainty also improves with κ\kappa but stays below the first-token uncertainty at every κ\kappa. Agreement has the highest F1 for κ≤90\kappa\leq 90, and its F1 levels off at about .865 from κ=50\kappa=50. The verbalized signals perform worst, below the baseline at every κ\kappa.

Against the baselines, the margin for GPT-4o mini is modest (at κ=210\kappa=210, accuracy .814 for first-token uncertainty against .740 for the majority class and .806 for the meta-model) but larger for Llama-3.1-8B (.802 against .638 and .750) and Qwen3-8B (.729 against .544 and .705). Most errors lie near τ\tau (Figure 2b): after excluding the datasets within .025 of τ\tau, HGB with uncertainty is the best method for every LLM, and the farther the remaining datasets are from τ\tau, the more often it is correct (Appendix F).

We then train the estimator by adding one signal at a time, family by family, in three orders that each start from a different family (Figure 2a). From κ=130\kappa=130 onward the three orders show the same pattern. Again the internal probability signals contribute the most: the performance changes little when label consistency is added after them, and rises the most when they are added later. The verbalized signals give the lowest starting performance, which even declines as κ\kappa grows, and mostly lower the performance when they come later. The label consistency signal gives a modest starting performance at small κ\kappa, and adding the internal probability signals after it helps at larger κ\kappa.

Conclusion

Our results show that signals from a small sample of instances (less than 150) labeled by the LLM can support the decision of whether to use zero-shot annotation. Among the signals, internal probabilities are the most useful, and the first-token uncertainty alone matches or outperforms the full signal set. Practitioners should prefer models that expose token probabilities when possible; if these are not available, we find that self-agreement is a better predictor than verbalized confidence.

Limitations

We construct two task families which allow us to derive ground truth from metadata. The advantage of this approach is that we can understand LLM performance in a setting with little label noise; the topic codes and genre tags are still human-assigned, and we observe that disagreement about them is plausibly higher for closely related pairs. However, future work should re-apply our approach to a larger and more varied collection of datasets: our estimator is always trained on gold-labeled datasets from the same two task families and prompt format as the test dataset (with disjoint texts), so transfer to an unrelated task is untested. We also do not compare against hand-labeling the κ\kappa sampled instances, the natural alternative when some annotation budget exists, and our standard errors reflect variation across three seeds, not across datasets. In addition, following prior work, we define reliability through accuracy at a fixed threshold. In scenarios where other aspects of performance matter more, such as performance on a minority class, other metrics like F1 could serve as the reliability measure instead. We test three LLMs and the relative usefulness of the signals already differs among them (see Appendix F) and may differ further for other models or decoding settings. Finally, we study only binary text classification; tasks with more labels or free-form outputs, such as spans or summaries, may call for different signals.

Appendix A Annotation Prompt and Signals

Every annotation run sends the system and user prompts in Figure 3. The bracketed fields are filled with the dataset’s task description, its two labels with their definitions, and the label names (Table 3 shows two datasets), and with the instance’s text, which is a headline for the NYT topic pairs and a script or its truncation for the genre pairs.

GPT-4o mini (gpt-4o-mini-2024-07-18) is queried through the OpenAI API in JSON mode, with the log-probability of every output token returned. Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen3-8B run locally with vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023), with JSON output enforced during decoding, a top-pp of 1, and at most 128 output tokens. Qwen3-8B runs with its thinking mode turned off, and the 1,056 instances whose prompts exceed its default context of 40,960 tokens are run with YaRN context extension (Peng et al., 2024). Each instance is labeled k=5k=5 times at temperature 1.

To read the log-probabilities of the label, we locate the value of the "label" field in the output and take the tokens that overlap it: uncertaintyfirst\operatorname{uncertainty}_{\mathrm{first}} uses the first of these tokens and uncertaintyavg\operatorname{uncertainty}_{\text{avg}} the mean over all of them. For the open-weight LLMs, these are the log-probabilities of the model’s raw output distribution, before temperature scaling. The verbalized signals are the values of the "confidence" and "stability" fields, clipped to [0,1][0,1].

Appendix B Datasets

For the NYT topic pairs, each of the 27 topics contributes 150 front-page articles, and the dataset for a pair of topics contains the 150 articles of each. All 351 NYT datasets thus have 300 instances with balanced labels, and the LLM sees only the headline.

For the sliding-window genre pairs, Table 2 lists the 11 pairs. A pair uses the movies tagged with exactly one of its two genres. We drop movies whose scraped script is shorter than 500 characters, which leaves 247–287 movies per pair, and some pairs are unbalanced (e.g., 38 romance and 249 drama movies).

Table 3 shows the task description, the label definitions, and one instance of a dataset from each family. Figure 4 shows how dataset accuracy is distributed for each LLM.

Appendix C Grouped Cross-Validation

Our datasets share texts. Each NYT topic contributes the same 150 articles to all 26 of its pairs, the ten lengths of a genre pair contain the same movies, and since a movie can carry several genre tags, different genre pairs can also share movies. Leaving out one dataset at a time would therefore leave test texts in the training data, so we build folds in which no test text appears in training.

For the NYT topic pairs, we shuffle the 27 topics into 9 groups of 3. For each pair of groups (A,B)(A,B), including A=BA=B, the test set is every NYT dataset whose two topics fall in AA and BB, and the training set is every NYT dataset with neither topic in AA or BB, plus all genre datasets. For the genre pairs, each fold tests one genre pair at all ten lengths and trains on all NYT datasets plus the genre pairs that share neither genre with it. Because these pairs can still share movies, each training dataset drops the instances whose text also appears in the test set. This gives 45+11=5645+11=56 folds, and every dataset is tested exactly once.

In each fold, gg and its cutoff tt are fitted on κ\kappa instances sampled from each training dataset, and each test dataset is scored on κ\kappa instances sampled from it. Since every dataset is tested once, we pool the estimates of all 461 datasets and compute accuracy and F1 once per seed. The three seeds (42, 43, and 44) change the topic groups and every sampled set of instances.

Appendix D Instance-Level Classifiers

For the instance-level classifier gg we test SVM, HGB, and XGBoost. HGB is histogram-based gradient boosting with 200 iterations. XGBoost uses 200 trees of depth at most 6 and a learning rate of 0.1.

Appendix E Baselines

We compare our estimator with ATC (Garg et al., 2022) and the meta-model of Fu et al. (2023). Both see the same folds and the same κ\kappa instances per dataset as our estimator, and use only the gold labels of the training datasets’ sampled instances. Both need a confidence score for each instance, and we use exp⁡(−uncertaintyavg⁡(xi))\exp(-\operatorname{uncertainty}_{\text{avg}}(x_{i})) as the closest of our signals to the label probability these methods use.

Figure 5 shows where the three methods go wrong at κ=210\kappa=210. For GPT-4o mini and Qwen3-8B the three methods are close, and most of their mistakes fall in the bins next to τ\tau. For Llama-3.1-8B, ATC does worst, predicting 42–55% of the datasets in each truly unreliable bin as reliable. Our estimator predicts more of the truly reliable datasets as reliable (61–96% below the top bin, against 40–70% for the meta-model).

Appendix F Full Results

Table 4 compares our estimator with the prior methods after excluding the datasets closest to τ\tau, it reports metrics at κ=210\kappa=210 after excluding the datasets with .01, .025 and .05 of τ\tau, with the baseline recomputed on the remaining datasets.

Tables 5–7 give accuracy and F1 for every combination of instance-level classifier and signal set, one table per LLM. Figure 6 shows the three signal orders of Figure 2a for all three LLMs.

From κ=130\kappa=130 on, the first-token uncertainty is the best single signal for every LLM and classifier, in both accuracy and F1, and with it alone the three classifiers are within .036 of each other. Combining all five signals beats the first-token uncertainty alone at most κ\kappa only for Llama-3.1-8B. The verbalized signals stay below the F1 baseline at every κ\kappa for GPT-4o mini and Llama-3.1-8B; for Qwen3-8B, stability is at or slightly above it.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.

Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a list of packages that need conversion, and welcome developer contributions.
